name: The Lump of Labour Fallacy
statement: There is no fixed amount of work to share out, so one group working more need not leave less for others.
statementAccent: no fixed amount of work to share out
meaning: The lump of labour fallacy is the alleged error of assuming there is a fixed amount of work, a 'lump', to be done in an economy, so that if one group does more of it, immigrants, machines, pieceworkers, or those working longer hours, correspondingly less is left for everyone else. Mainstream economists argue this reasoning is generally mistaken because the quantity of work is not fixed: labour demand adjusts, new spending creates new jobs, and productivity gains raise incomes that are spent elsewhere, so employment is not a zero-sum quantity.
mechanism: The claimed error is treating the total amount of work as a constant to be divided, when in fact it responds to conditions. When new workers arrive or machines raise output, the extra production generates income that is spent, which raises demand for other goods and the labour to make them. Cheaper or more plentiful output expands markets rather than exhausting a fixed stock of tasks. Over the long run and in aggregate, the economy has repeatedly absorbed large increases in the workforce and in productivity without permanent mass unemployment, which is the empirical backbone of the argument.

examples.text: The worry that immigrants 'take jobs' from natives assumes a fixed lump; the counter is that new workers also earn and spend, expanding the economy and the total number of jobs.

The fear that machines cause permanent mass unemployment is the automation-specific form; US farm employment fell from around two-fifths of the workforce in 1900 to a few percent by 2000 without lasting mass joblessness.
The idea that shorter work-weeks or early retirement 'free up' jobs for others treats work as a fixed lump to be redistributed, the application the fallacy's critics most dispute.

variants.name: The Luddite fallacy
variants.text: The name given to the automation-specific version, the claim that technological change destroys jobs on net, treated as the same underlying error applied to machines rather than people.

variants.name: The fallacy of the fallacy
variants.text: Tom Walker's argument, echoing Pigou and Dobb, that branding every such claim a simple fallacy is itself a refutation that misses the point, since real short-run and local displacement can occur.

whyItMatters: It is one of the most frequently invoked heuristics in public debate over immigration, automation, trade, women's entry into the workforce, and the length of the working week, and it remains prominent in current argument over artificial intelligence and jobs. Its role is partly analytical and partly rhetorical: it is deployed to characterise an opponent's position as resting on an obvious economic error, which makes understanding both its force and its contested status important for anyone weighing those debates.

working.text: when an argument assumes more work by one group means less for others, ask whether the total quantity of work is really fixed.
follow the income that new workers or new output generate, since it creates demand and jobs elsewhere in the economy.
acknowledge that specific workers, occupations, or regions can genuinely lose out even when aggregate long-run employment adjusts.

limits: It is a heuristic argument, not a settled theorem, and the blanket application of the 'fallacy' label is itself academically disputed. Labour demand is not infinitely elastic, and short-run and local displacement effects are real: particular workers, occupations, or regions genuinely can and do lose out even if aggregate long-run employment adjusts. Critics from Pigou and Dobb to Tom Walker argue the charge is often used to dismiss arguments, especially for shorter hours, without actually refuting them. The aggregate, long-run case is powerful and often correct, but it is silent about who bears the transitional costs.
misreadings: It is not a proven law but a contested heuristic, and its sweeping use to label every concern a 'fallacy' is disputed. Schloss did not coin it to attack shorter working hours; his original target was workers restricting their piece-work output, and the application to work-time reduction is a later extension that its critics reject. And 'no fixed lump' does not mean immigration or automation never costs anyone a job; the aggregate, long-run argument does not deny real short-run or localised displacement, nor does it claim unemployment can never rise over the business cycle.
origin: The term was coined by the English economist David Frederick Schloss in his 1891 article 'Why Working-Men Dislike Piece-Work' in The Economic Review, describing workers who restricted output in the belief that a fixed amount of work existed; its status as a fallacy has since been challenged by Pigou, Dobb, and Tom Walker.

sources.text: Lump of labour fallacy, Wikipedia. — the fixed-work misconception, its applications, and Schloss's coinage.

Schloss, 'Why Working-Men Dislike Piece-Work,' The Economic Review, Vol. I, No. 3 (1891), pp. 311-326 (transcription). — the original naming of 'the theory of the Lump of Labour' among output-restricting pieceworkers.
